code.title: DRY: one home for a rule

followUps:
Take two checks that look the same today: one validates a 10-digit phone number, the other a 10-digit invoice number. Someone merges them into one isTenDigits() helper. Later phones must accept a +91 prefix, and the change breaks invoice numbers. They matched only by chance because they change for different reasons.

Test before merging: if rule X changes, must Y change too? If not, keep them apart. The rule of three (wait for the third copy) helps.

You undo it in two steps: inline the shared function back into each caller, then re-extract only the part that is truly common.

  1. Copy the body into every call site and delete the flags and parameters that only served one caller.
  2. Each caller is now simple and correct on its own.
  3. Look again: whatever is still identical and changes for the same reason becomes a small new function.

Duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction, so this is a good trade. Do it with tests green after each step.

code.title: KISS vs over-engineering (YAGNI)
code.python:
# KISS: the simplest code that meets today's need.
def simple(price):
    return price - price // 10

# Over-engineered: a registry of policies although only one exists (YAGNI).
registry = {"default": lambda p: p - p // 10}

price = 200
print("price=%d" % price)
print("simple     = %d (1 function)" % simple(price))
print("engineered = %d (registry + lookup + key)" % registry["default"](price))
print("same answer, more to read and maintain")

followUps:
I would not apply YAGNI to one-way-door decisions, things that are very costly to change later. Examples are the shape of stored data, a public API that other teams call, and security basics such as authentication and encryption.

Adding a column to a table later is easy, but getting a published API contract wrong breaks every client. Also never skip tests, clear names or refactoring in its name: those keep future change cheap, which is what makes deferring features safe in the first place.

I ask questions instead of saying "no", and I tie them to cost.

  • Which requirement needs this extension point today? Name the ticket.
  • What is the cheapest change if we add it later? If it is one small refactor, we wait.
  • Cost of carry: every reader must understand it, and Fowler's "cost of repair" applies if the real need differs.

I suggest the simplest version and leave a note. If it is a one-way door (public API, data model), I accept some thinking ahead.

code.title: Inheritance double-counting vs composition
code.python:
class Bag:
    def __init__(self):
        self.items = []
    def add(self, x):
        self.items.append(x)
    def add_all(self, xs):
        for x in xs:          # calls self.add: an internal detail
            self.add(x)

class CountingBag(Bag):       # inheritance: counts adds, add_all counted twice
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.count = 0
    def add(self, x):
        self.count += 1
        super().add(x)
    def add_all(self, xs):
        self.count += len(xs)
        super().add_all(xs)

class CountingWrapper:        # composition: uses only Bag's public contract
    def __init__(self):
        self.inner = Bag()
        self.count = 0
    def add_all(self, xs):
        self.count += len(xs)
        self.inner.add_all(xs)

xs = [1, 2, 3]
print("added 3 items")
a = CountingBag(); a.add_all(xs)
print("inheritance count = %d (wrong)" % a.count)
w = CountingWrapper(); w.add_all(xs)
print("composition count = %d (right)" % w.count)

followUps:
The fragile base class problem is when a child class breaks because the parent class changed its internals, even though the parent's public methods look the same.

Concrete case: a child overrides add and addAll to count items. The parent's addAll happens to call add in a loop. Adding 3 items now counts 3 in addAll plus 3 in add, giving 6. If the parent later stops calling add, the count silently becomes 3. The child depended on a private detail.

They make composition with forwarding cheap, so you do not write all the delegating methods by hand.

In Kotlin, class Counted(inner: Bag) : Bag by inner auto-generates every method of Bag as a call to inner, and you override only the ones you want to change. Lombok's @Delegate on a field does the same for Java. You still get composition (using only the public contract), but without the boilerplate that makes people reach for inheritance.

code.title: Measuring cohesion with LCOM
code.python:
# Each method is a bit mask of the fields it uses: items=1, printer=2, user=4.
names = ["total", "addItem", "print", "setPrinter", "login", "logout"]
uses = [1, 1, 2, 2, 4, 4]
sharing = not_sharing = 0
for i in range(len(uses)):
    for j in range(i + 1, len(uses)):
        # a pair "shares" if both touch at least one common field
        if uses[i] & uses[j]:
            sharing += 1
        else:
            not_sharing += 1
print("methods=%d pairs=%d" % (len(names), sharing + not_sharing))
print("sharing=%d notSharing=%d" % (sharing, not_sharing))
print("LCOM=%d (high: three unrelated groups, split the class)" % max(0, not_sharing - sharing))

followUps:
From worst (strongest) to best (weakest) coupling:

  1. Content: one module changes another's internals or private data.
  2. Common: both share global state.
  3. External: both depend on one outside format or vendor.
  4. Control: one passes a flag that steers the other's logic.
  5. Stamp: passing a whole structure when only part is needed.
  6. Data: passing only the needed values.

Message coupling (calls through a narrow interface) is the best.

LCOM (Lack of Cohesion of Methods) counts how many method pairs in a class use no common field. A high number means the class holds unrelated groups and should probably be split.

Example: 6 methods give 15 pairs. If only 3 pairs share a field, LCOM1 = 12 - 3 = 9, so the class is poorly cohesive. Limits: getters and setters distort it, fields used by every method hide problems, and a class with no fields scores oddly. It needs human judgement, not a pass/fail gate.

code.title: Law of Demeter: tell, don't ask

followUps:
Deep mock chains in a test are the warning sign: if you must write when(order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity()), you have to mock three objects just to test one line.

The code under test knows too much about the object graph. With a method like order.shippingCity() the test mocks one call. So hard-to-test code and Law of Demeter violations usually show up together, and the test pain tells you where to add a delegating method.

Add a delegating method only when it expresses a real domain idea, not just to hide a dot.

Good: order.shippingCity() or account.isOverdrawn(), because they name a business question. Bad: a class whose methods all just forward to another (a Middle Man) and add nothing. If you find many forwarders, let the caller talk to the inner object directly, or move the behaviour that uses the data into that inner class. Data-only records are fine to chain through.

code.title: Refactor safely with a characterization check

followUps:
As small as possible: one refactoring step per commit, and the tests must be green at every commit.

A good size is one rename, one Extract Method, or one move, which a reviewer can check in under a minute and which is easy to revert. For the 300-line method that means perhaps 20 to 30 small commits. If a step breaks tests and the cause is not obvious, undo it and take a smaller step. Never mix refactoring with behaviour changes in the same commit.

Show the cost of not doing it, and make the work small and visible.

  • Boy Scout rule: leave the code a little cleaner each time you touch it, as part of the feature estimate.
  • Hotspots: use git history to find the files that change often and cause bugs, and only refactor those. Example: a file changed 120 times last year with 4 bugs is worth a day; stable ugly code is not.
  • Report results: fewer bugs, faster reviews, shorter build times.

code.title: Shotgun surgery vs one class per payment method

followUps:
Divergent change breaks the Single Responsibility Principle, and shotgun surgery breaks cohesion in the other direction (knowledge scattered).

Divergent change: a class with many reasons to change violates SRP. Shotgun surgery: one idea spread over many classes breaks Open/Closed (adding a type means editing many places), and also high cohesion and DRY. Fixing both leads to Dependency Inversion: code depends on an interface, and each new payment method is a new class.

Change coupling: files that keep changing together in the same commits are probably one idea split into pieces.

Run git log --name-only and count how often each pair of files appears in the same commit. If Checkout.java, Refund.java and Report.java appear together in 18 of 20 feature commits, that is shotgun surgery. Tools such as code-maat do this counting. Then gather the shared knowledge into one class.

code.title: Money as a value object

followUps:
Use long minor units (such as paise or cents) for most money code, and BigDecimal when you need arbitrary precision or many decimal places.

Store 500.50 as 50050 in a long: it is exact, fast and simple to add. Division and percentages need an explicit rounding rule. BigDecimal carries its own scale and rounding mode, so it suits tax and interest. Never use double: 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. Wrap either choice inside a Money value object.

The cost is usually negligible, and the safety is worth far more.

Small short-lived objects are cheap to allocate on modern runtimes, and the JIT can often remove the allocation entirely (escape analysis). Only measure if profiling shows a hot loop with millions of objects, then use primitives inside that one loop and keep the value object at the boundary. Java's planned value classes (Project Valhalla) aim to remove even that cost, so you keep the clean design.

code.title: Injecting a gateway and a clock

followUps:
Constructor injection is the default: it makes dependencies required, visible and the object always fully built.

  • Constructor: the object cannot exist without its dependencies, fields can be final, and tests see exactly what to supply.
  • Setter: only for truly optional dependencies; the object can be half-built.
  • Field: hides dependencies, needs reflection or a container to test, and allows no immutability.

A constructor with 7 parameters is a useful smell: the class likely does too much.

A static method is fine when it is a pure function: same input always gives the same output, with no hidden state, no I/O and no time.

Examples: Math.max(3, 7) is always 7, Collections.sort on its argument, a string formatter. They need no fake because they cannot surprise you. A static method becomes a problem when it reads the clock, the network, a global setting or a singleton, because the test cannot control it.

code.title: Connascence of position vs name

followUps:
Connascence of position is when callers must remember the order of arguments, so a swap compiles but is wrong.

Example: transfer(String from, String to, int amount) called as transfer("B", "A", 5) moves money the wrong way and no compiler complains. Fix: pass a parameter object (new TransferRequest(src, dst, amount) with named fields), use keyword arguments in Python, or use distinct types such as AccountId and Amount. That turns position into name or type, which is weaker.

The common ones are connascence of meaning, of algorithm, of timing, and of value.

  • Meaning: both services agree that status = 3 means "shipped". Use shared enums or string names in a schema.
  • Algorithm: both sides must hash or sign identically; publish one library or spec.
  • Timing: service B needs A's data to exist first; use events and retries.
  • Value: duplicated config must stay equal.

Keep it weak across services: names and types in a versioned contract.

code.title: One factory switch, then polymorphism

followUps:
The expression problem is the trade-off that you can easily add new types or easily add new operations, but not both at once without extra machinery.

With classes and polymorphism, adding a new type (Hexagon) is one new class, but adding a new operation (perimeter()) means editing every class. With a closed set of types and a switch or visitor, adding an operation is one new function, but adding a type means editing every switch. Choose by which axis changes more often.

With a closed hierarchy the compiler can check that you handled every case, so adding a new type turns forgotten places into compile errors instead of silent bugs.

A Java sealed interface with a pattern-matching switch (or a TypeScript discriminated union) must cover every subtype, so no default is needed. An enum switch with a default hides a new constant: it falls into default at runtime and may return a wrong answer. Avoid default when you want exhaustiveness.

code.title: Finding refactoring hotspots (churn x complexity)
code.python:
files = ["Order.java", "Billing.java", "Legacy.java", "Utils.java", "Mailer.java"]
changes = [120, 95, 2, 80, 10]      # commits in the last year (from git log)
complexity = [45, 70, 90, 20, 30]   # e.g. cyclomatic complexity
score = [c * x for c, x in zip(changes, complexity)]   # churn x complexity
order = sorted(range(len(files)), key=lambda i: -score[i])   # highest first
for k, i in enumerate(order):
    print("%d. %s changes=%d complexity=%d score=%d" % (k + 1, files[i], changes[i], complexity[i], score[i]))
print("refactor first: %s (Legacy.java is ugly but stable)" % files[order[0]])

followUps:
Agree on the order using data and business risk, and use small amounts of time for each refactor, not a big project.

  • Show hotspots: the files that change most and cause the most defects.
  • Attach refactoring to upcoming features that touch those files, so the work is part of the estimate.
  • Reserve a small steady budget, for example 10 to 20 percent of each sprint, instead of asking for a "refactoring month".
  • Explain in business terms: shorter delivery time for the next feature, fewer incidents.

Measure things that show up in delivery speed and quality, not code beauty.

  • Lead time to ship a change in the hotspot area (days).
  • Defect rate and incident count from that module.
  • Change coupling: how many files a typical feature touches.
  • Complexity and churn of the top 5 hotspots, trending down.
  • Build and test time.

If a feature that used to touch 12 files now touches 3, the work is paying off.

A rewrite is justified only when the old system cannot be changed safely and the cost of keeping it clearly exceeds a rewrite.

Examples: the technology is unsupported with no security patches, the platform cannot meet a hard requirement (scale, compliance), nobody understands the code and no tests can be added, or the domain has changed so much that the old model no longer fits. Even then, prefer replacing it piece by piece (strangler fig) so you ship value continuously and can stop at any time.

Write short, concrete rules and focus review on what AI gets wrong most often.

  • Author owns it: the person who prompts must understand and explain every line.
  • Check for hidden behaviour changes mixed into "cleanups", and for duplicated rules and single-implementation interfaces.
  • Require tests that fail before and pass after the change.
  • Keep diffs small; split large generated changes.
  • Verify that calls to libraries and APIs actually exist.

Review for design (coupling, naming), not just whether it runs.

Behaviour-preserving, mechanical changes that tests can verify: renames, extracting a method, moving a class, formatting, replacing a magic number with a constant.

I would trust an agent with these only when characterization tests exist and run in CI, the diff is small, and the change is separate from feature work. I would not leave unattended: changes to public APIs, data models, security code, concurrency, or anything that crosses service boundaries. A human reviews every diff before merge.
